item.title: Kyoto Cherry Blossom Season: Where and When for Sakura — Guide
item.description: Cherry blossom season transforms Kyoto into one of the most beautiful cities on earth for a fleeting week or two, usually in late March and early April. The old capital is arguably the finest place in Japan to see sakura, precisely because the blossom is set against temples, pagodas, canals and traditional streets rather than modern buildings. The Philosopher’s Path, the Okazaki canal, Maruyama Park’s weeping cherry, the grounds of Ninnaji and Daigoji, and the riverbanks all become famous scenes, many floodlit at night.

item.title: Izumi Nature Park Cherry Blossom Guide: Sakura & Access
item.description: When spring arrives in the rural Boso interior, Izumi Nature Park near Sosa becomes one of Chiba’s loveliest cherry-blossom (sakura) spots — a quiet expanse of ponds, woods and meadows where rows of cherry trees bloom alongside golden rapeseed flowers for a classic pink-and-yellow spring scene. Far from the city crowds, it’s a peaceful place for hanami picnics, gentle walks and birdwatching, and it pairs perfectly with the Isumi Railway, whose little trains roll through the same flower-filled countryside.

item.title: Okinawa Cherry Blossoms Guide: Japan's First Sakura (Jan–Feb)
item.description: Okinawa sees Japan’s first cherry blossoms of the year — blooming in January and February, weeks ahead of the mainland. The island’s sakura is the kanhizakura (hikanzakura), a vivid, deep-pink bell-shaped cherry quite different from the pale Somei-Yoshino seen elsewhere. Set against subtropical green and historic castle walls, Okinawa’s early blossoms make for a uniquely warm-weather hanami, celebrated with cherry festivals in the north. It’s a wonderful reason to visit the island in winter.

item.title: Osaka Cherry Blossom Guide: Best Hanami Spots & Timing
item.description: For about two weeks each spring, Osaka turns pink. Cherry blossom (sakura) season transforms the castle moats, riverbanks, and parks into clouds of blossom, and the city throws itself into hanami — flower-viewing picnics under the trees, by day and (lit up) by night. From the iconic combination of blossoms and Osaka Castle to the riverside tunnels of the Kema Sakuranomiya and the once-a-year Japan Mint passage, Osaka has some of the Kansai region’s best and liveliest cherry-blossom spots.

item.title: Tokyo Cherry Blossom Guide: Best Hanami Spots, Timing & Etiquette
item.description: There is no week in the Japanese calendar more celebrated than sakura season. For about ten days each spring, Tokyo — a city of 14 million people — pivots its entire social life around sitting under trees. Friends, families, and colleagues converge on parks from early morning to claim prime spots, spread blue tarps, and spend the afternoon eating, drinking, and staring upward at a canopy of pale pink that will be completely gone in a week.

item.title: Tottori Events & Festivals: Shan-Shan Umbrella Dance, Crab Season & Seasonal Celebrations
item.description: Tottori is quiet by Japanese standards — that’s one of its virtues. But several times a year the prefecture comes alive with events that are genuinely worth planning a trip around. The Shan-Shan umbrella festival is one of Japan’s most distinctive summer celebrations. Matsuba crab season opening in November is a spectacle with real ritual attached to it. And the sand dunes at night, lit by seasonal illuminations, are something you can’t see anywhere else in the world.

item.title: Japan Spring Seasonal Guide: Must-Try Sakura Dishes
item.description: Spring Seasonal Food in Japan: The Complete Guide to Sakura Dishes & What to Eat This Season Spring in Japan is famous for cherry blossoms, but here’s what most visitors don’t realize: the food is just as spectacular as the flowers. Understanding spring seasonal food in Japan — from sakura dishes and delicate cherry blossom sweets to wild mountain vegetables and the first bonito catch — will transform your trip from a sightseeing itinerary into a full sensory experience.
